The golden rule: if a word ends in a vowel, -n or -s, the stress falls on the SECOND-TO-LAST syllable: tor-TI-lla, QUIE-ro, CO-men. Otherwise, on the LAST one: co-MER, be-BER, es-pa-ÑOL. Words that break the rule get a written accent: ja-MÓN, ca-FÉ.
Say LL like the “y” in “yes”: tortilla = “tor-tee-ya”, botella = “bo-te-ya”.
Quick diphthongs: cuenta = “kwen-ta”, quiero = “kye-ro”, in a single syllable.
Great news: most Spanish verbs are REGULAR. You learn one recipe and apply it to hundreds of verbs.
Step 1: take the infinitive (hablar). Step 2: cut off the ending -ar / -er / -ir (habl-). Step 3: add the ending for the person.
“Yo” always ends in -o: hablo, como, vivo, tomo, bebo. It’s the most used form, so learn it first.
Regular verbs you can use from today: tomar (to take, to have), trabajar (to work), estudiar (to study), beber (to drink), leer (to read), escribir (to write).
QUERER is “almost regular”: in 4 persons the e in the middle becomes ie. Only nosotros and vosotros stay normal.
For “I want to eat” you just add the infinitive, without “to”: “Quiero comer” = “I want to eat”.
In Spain people order directly, but with “por favor”. Here are the most common phrases:
Para mí, un café, por favor.
Could I have a water? (very Spanish)
“Tomar” = to have, to take. “¿Qué vas a tomar?” = “What are you having?” It’s used for both food and drink.
“El agua” is a feminine word (agua fría = cold water). It takes “el” only so that two “a” sounds don’t clash: “el agua”, but “las aguas”.
After 30, numbers are written as three words, with “y” (and) in the middle: 31 = treinta y uno, 45 = cuarenta y cinco, 99 = noventa y nueve.
Careful: “sesenta” (60) and “setenta” (70) look alike! SeSenta = Six(ty), SeTenta = SevenTy.
Prices: “23.50 €” is said “veintitrés euros con cincuenta” or simply “veintitrés cincuenta”.
“Me gusta” works backwards compared with English: literally “it pleases me”. The thing you like is the subject.
After “gusta” you put the article: “Me gusta EL café” (not “me gusta café”), even though English says “I like coffee” with no article.
On Saturday morning, Ana and Mihai go to the market to cook together.
On Saturday morning, Ana and Mihai go to the Cebada market.
Today they’re eating at Ana’s place and they want to cook a paella.
First they buy vegetables: tomatoes, peppers and an onion.
Ana asks: “How much is a kilo of tomatoes?”
The stallholder answers: “Two euros fifty.” That’s cheap.
Then they buy fish and prawns. The fish is expensive: eighteen euros.
Mihai also wants to buy fruit: apples and oranges.
There’s a little bar in the market. Ana and Mihai have a coffee.
Mihai says: “In Romania we eat lots of vegetables too, but we don’t eat paella.”
Ana answers: “So what do you eat in Romania?”
“We eat sarmale, mici and lots of sour soup. I really love ciorbă!”
In total, the shopping costs forty-three euros. They pay and go back home.
Today is Saturday and Mihai wants to cook a paella for Ana.
It’s his first paella and he’s a little nervous.
In the morning he goes to the market. He buys rice, tomatoes, chicken, peppers and a little fish.
The stallholder asks: “For a paella? What about saffron?”. Mihai doesn’t know what saffron is, but he buys it.
At home, Mihai reads the recipe on his phone. He chops the vegetables and puts oil in the pan.
Then he adds the rice, the water and the saffron. The kitchen smells wonderful!
But Mihai talks on the phone with his mother… for forty minutes.
When he goes back into the kitchen, the paella is black.
At two o’clock Ana arrives. She looks at the pan and says nothing. Then she laughs a lot.
“Never mind,” she says. “Let’s go to Kenji’s restaurant!”.
And they eat Japanese ramen. Mihai pays the bill.
Apply the recipe: cut off -ar / -er / -ir and add the ending.
How much is it? — Fifteen euros.

In Spain, many restaurants have a menu of the day.
The menu costs twelve or fifteen euros.
It has a first course, a second course and a dessert.
The first course is usually soup or salad.
The second course is meat or fish.
Bread and a drink are also included in the price.
Spaniards eat late: at two or three o’clock.
